extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students of political economy, social philosophy, and ethics (Victorian/19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles about what constitutes social progress, civilization, and moral conduct in commerce as argued in 19th‑century social-philosophical essays. Focuses on causes of progress/decay in societies and the moral roots and remedies of commercial dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress depends on association and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress goes on just as society tends toward closer association and greater equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilization advances when there is increased cooperation, union, and liberty — e.g., growth of larger and denser communities, commerce, international and municipal law, security of property and person, individual liberty, and democratic government are cited as markers of modern progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilizations that are socially homogeneous tend to petrify
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of complete petrifaction (social stagnation) depends on external causes; homogeneous civilizations with strong bonds of custom and superstition repress disintegrating forces as well as improvement and become easily conquered or remain static.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptian-type civilizations where masses are trained to passive acquiescence; such societies may be conquered and continue in the same order or be left in ruins with loss of knowledge and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispersion of power and social diversity foster progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Association of peoples who had acquired distinctive social characteristics, and the splitting up of concentrated power into many small centres, prevent domination and foster civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grecian petty republics and Roman small-holders (independent husbandmen/free citizens) are given as positive examples; influx of Northern nations and local sovereignty checks concentrated tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to inequality causes societal decay
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of inequality—concentration of wealth and power—dries up social strength and produces political, mental, moral, and material decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Rome’s decline (great estates, slavery, despotism, loss of learning) is attributed to inequality; measures to combat inequality (e.g., Grecian devices) are portrayed as essential to sustain civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions that promote association and equality are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (religious, legal, municipal) that prevent concentration of power and encourage rights and association support civilization’s growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christianity (papacy preventing spiritual concentration; celibacy limiting priestly caste), monastic orders, councils that ran across boundaries, and the Church’s early role in emancipation and uniting nations are cited as institutional supports for association and equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce, law, and security as measures of modern civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The expansion of commerce, municipal and international law, secure property and personal liberty, and democratic government are concrete indicators of a superior modern civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are linked to the freeing of mental power, scientific discovery, and technological invention — i.e., they are both means and measures of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: War and slavery are generally anti-association and hinder progress
rubrics_metrics.description: War, being the opposite of association, can only aid progress when it prevents further war or breaks antisocial barriers; slavery always hampers and prevents progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author rejects doctrines that war/slavery promote progress; slavery wastes human power, prevents invention, and stifles utilization of discoveries even when made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom (not slavery) is the condition of invention and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: No slave-holding people are inventive; freedom gives the capacity to develop discoveries and harness natural forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical contrast: classical world’s literary polish without corresponding technological invention is attributed to universal slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law: social adjustments must promote justice and equal liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of human progress is the moral law: social arrangements that promote justice, equality of rights, and liberty (bounded by equal liberty of others) are what allow civilization to advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political economy and social science are subsumed under moral principles exemplified in religious teachings about equality and mutual regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success often incompatible with strict integrity under competitive pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: In many trades, success appears incompatible with strict integrity because traders must conform to the prevailing commercial code or be ruined; intense competition incentivizes cutting ethical corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author observes that those who sink below the commercial ethical standard are expelled and those who exceed it are pulled down or ruined; metaphor: 'Cheat and be cheated' / 'commercial cannibalism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Indiscriminate public admiration of wealth is a chief cause of commercial dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The intense desire for wealth — fueled by society’s respect for wealth and external signs of success — is the principal inciter of mercantile malpractices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social rewards (deference, status, invitations, civic honours) given to wealth regardless of how it was acquired pressure traders into dishonest practices to maintain appearances and social position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral restraint varies with the vividness of perceived harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The keenness of sympathy with the pain inflicted is the ultimate moral restraint; people are less inhibited about actions that cause remote or diffuse harms than about actions causing immediate, visible suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why petty indirect frauds increase while gross direct theft declines — remote victims and subtle harms elicit weaker sympathies and restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small and indirect frauds can increase even if gross frauds decline
rubrics_metrics.description: While large direct frauds may be decreasing, subtle and indirect commercial dishonesties (adulteration, deceptive measures, joint-stock bank deceptions) have increased in variety and number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern is consistent with an overall rise in morality if public attention and sensitivity to certain harms differ in scale and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressures (competition, non-payment, customer injustice) contribute to unethical practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes such as relentless competition, customers demanding price reductions, and non-payment by wealthier customers push traders toward illegitimate means to survive financially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include retailers naming prices higher than intended to allow bargaining, large shopkeepers ruined by unpunctual customers, and shopkeepers resorting to adulteration to cut costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion must equally condemn direct and indirect theft to purify trade morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for commercial vices is a purified public opinion that regards adulteration, over-trading, exaggerated reports, repudiation of guarantees, etc., as akin to pickpocketing and treats perpetrators with similar disdain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when society's abhorrence extends to thefts of all degrees of indirectness will mercantile vices disappear; author is pessimistic about rapid change but advocates vigorous protest against adoration of mere success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and applaud rightly-acquired wealth, condemn dishonest wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for wealth is proper when it evidences intelligence, energy, self-control, or public benefit; but admiration must be discriminating and refuse homage to wealth gained by dishonourable means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right acquisition and proper use of wealth should be admired because they signal ability and public benefit (e.g., efficient manufacturers, judicious land improvement). Uncritical admiration of external symbols fosters corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible social approval/disapproval powerfully shapes moral behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward applause of peers is a stronger stimulus than abstract exhortations; visible approval of the rich (even if dishonest) neutralizes moral teaching and encourages continued malpractice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a dishonest rich man being twice elected mayor, or receiving civic honours, will feel emboldened despite sermons; conversely social derision (e.g., dressing as a dustman) deters behaviour.
